concepts: Arithmetic progression (five terms in symmetric form)
questions.question: Five numbers are in A.P., whose sum is $25$ and product is $2520$. If one of these five numbers is $-\frac{1}{2}$, then the greatest number amongst them is :
questions.key_idea: Take the terms as $a-2d,\ldots,a+2d$; the sum gives $a=5$ and the product becomes a quadratic in $d^2$.
solution: Let the five numbers in A.P. be $a-2d,\ a-d,\ a,\ a+d,\ a+2d$.
One of the terms is $-\frac{1}{2}$: with $d=\pm1$ the terms are $3,4,5,6,7$, so $-\frac12$ is not there; with $d=\frac{11}{2}$, $a-d=-\frac{1}{2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the given term first: it fixes $d$ directly, and the product only has to be checked.
solution: Reversing the order of an A.P. changes the sign of $d$, so take $d>0$; the mean is $a=5$ (sum $=25$).
The term $-\frac12$ is below the mean, so it is $5-d$ or $5-2d$.
If $5-d=-\frac12$ then $d=\frac{11}{2}$ and the numbers are $-6,-\frac12,5,\frac{21}{2},16$.
If $5-2d=-\frac12$ then $d=\frac{11}{4}$; the term $5-d=\frac94$ is positive and $5-2d<0$ makes the product negative, so it cannot be $2520$.
Hence $d=\frac{11}{2}$ and the greatest number is $5+2d=16$.

useful_results: Five terms in A.P.: write them as $a-2d,\ldots,a+2d$; the sum is $5a$ (the middle term is the mean).
For any odd number of terms in A.P. use the symmetric form, so the product becomes a function of $d^2$.
A given term of the A.P. fixes $d$ at once ($a\pm d$ or $a\pm2d$); a sign check of the product then removes the false case.
Instance here: $-6,\,-\frac12,\,5,\,\frac{21}{2},\,16$ has sum $25$ and product $2520$.

concepts: Arithmetic progression (sum of series with alternate terms)
questions.question: If the sum of the first $40$ terms of the series $3+4+8+9+13+14+18+19+\ldots$ is $(102)m$, then $m$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Terms at odd and even positions form two separate A.P.s with common difference $5$, $20$ terms each.
solution: Terms at odd positions are in A.P.: $3,8,13,\ldots$
Terms at even positions are in another A.P.: $4,9,14,\ldots$

alternate_solutions.idea: Group the terms in consecutive pairs $(3+4),(8+9),\ldots$: the pair sums form one A.P.
solution: The pair sums are $7,17,27,\ldots$, an A.P. with first term $7$ and common difference $10$.

useful_results: A series that alternates two patterns is either two interleaved progressions (split by position) or one progression of pair-blocks; choose the grouping that gives a single A.P.
If the sum of the $k$-th pair is $p_k$ and the pairs are in A.P., then $S_{2n}=\frac{n}{2}\left(2p_1+(n-1)D\right)$.
Instance: pair sums $7,17,27,\ldots$; $S_{40}=2040=102\times20$.

concepts: Infinite geometric series and trigonometric identities
questions.question: If $x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\tan^{2n}\theta$ and $y=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\cos^{2n}\theta$, $0<\theta<\frac{\pi}{4}$, then :
questions.key_idea: Both are infinite G.P.s with $|r|<1$: $x=\cos^2\theta$ and $y=\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Test one admissible value, $\theta=\frac{\pi}{6}$, and see which relation survives.

useful_results: $\sum_{n\ge0}r^n=\frac{1}{1-r}$ for $|r|<1$; here $r=-\tan^2\theta$ and $r=\cos^2\theta$ both lie in $(-1,1)$ for $0<\theta<\frac\pi4$.
$\frac{1}{1+\tan^2\theta}=\cos^2\theta$ and $\frac{1}{1-\cos^2\theta}=\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta$ turn the G.P. sums into trigonometric functions.
Identity-type options can be eliminated by substituting one convenient angle in the allowed range.

concepts: Sum to infinity of a series (geometric progressions)
questions.question: If $|x|<1$, $|y|<1$ and $x\ne y$, then the sum to infinity of the series $(x+y)+(x^2+xy+y^2)+(x^3+x^2y+xy^2+y^3)+\ldots$ is :
questions.key_idea: Multiply and divide by $x-y$: each bracket becomes $\frac{x^{n}-y^{n}}{x-y}$, so the series splits into two G.P.s.
solution: Each bracket is $\frac{x^{n}-y^{n}}{x-y}$, so the series is $\frac{x^2-y^2}{x-y}+\frac{x^3-y^3}{x-y}+\frac{x^4-y^4}{x-y}+\ldots\infty$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The brackets together contain every monomial $x^iy^j$ except $1$ exactly once, so the sum is a product of two G.P.s minus $1$.
solution: The $n$-th bracket is the sum of all monomials $x^iy^j$ with $i+j=n$ ($n=1,2,3,\ldots$).
Over all $n\ge1$ every pair $(i,j)\ne(0,0)$ of non-negative integers occurs exactly once.
This is option (C), the same answer (and it does not even need $x\ne y$).

useful_results: $x^n+x^{n-1}y+\ldots+y^n=\frac{x^{n+1}-y^{n+1}}{x-y}$ for $x\ne y$.
$\sum_{n\ge0}h_n(x,y)=\frac{1}{(1-x)(1-y)}$ for $|x|,|y|<1$, where $h_n$ is the sum of all monomials of degree $n$; so $\sum_{n\ge1}h_n=\frac{x+y-xy}{(1-x)(1-y)}$.
Check at $y=0$: the series is $x+x^2+\ldots=\frac{x}{1-x}$, which agrees with the formula.

concepts: Arithmetic progression (sum of terms, sub-progression)
questions.question: If the sum of first $11$ terms of an A.P., $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots$ is $0$ $(a_1\ne0)$, then the sum of the A.P., $a_1,a_3,a_5,\ldots,a_{23}$ is $ka_1$, where $k$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $S_{11}=0$ links $a_1$ and $d$; the odd-numbered terms form a new A.P. with $12$ terms and difference $2d$.
solution: $a_1,a_3,\ldots,a_{23}$ form another A.P.: number of terms $=12$, first term $=a$, common difference $=2d$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $S_{11}=0$ means the middle term $a_6$ is $0$, so $a_n=(n-6)d$ and the new A.P. is read off from its mean.
solution: $S_{11}=11\,a_6=0$ (mean of an A.P. of $11$ terms is its middle term), so $a_6=0$ and $a_n=(n-6)d$.
The $12$ terms $a_1,a_3,\ldots,a_{23}$ are an A.P. with mean $\frac{a_1+a_{23}}{2}=\frac{-5d+17d}{2}=6d$.
With $d=-\frac{a_1}{5}$: sum $=-\frac{72}{5}a_1$, so $k=-\frac{72}{5}$, the same answer.

useful_results: Sum of an A.P. $=$ (number of terms) $\times$ (mean) and the mean is the middle term (or the average of first and last).
If $S_{2m+1}=0$ then the middle term $a_{m+1}=0$ and $a_n=(n-m-1)d$.
Taking every second term of an A.P. gives an A.P. with difference $2d$ (every $k$-th term: $kd$).
Instance: $a_n=(n-6)d$; $a_1+a_3+\ldots+a_{23}=72d$.

concepts: Sum of series (geometric and arithmetic progressions combined)
questions.question: Let $S$ be the sum of the first $9$ terms of the series : $\{x+ka\}+\{x^2+(k+2)a\}+\{x^3+(k+4)a\}+\{x^4+(k+6)a\}+\ldots$ where $a\ne0$ and $x\ne1$. If $S=\frac{x^{10}-x+45a(x-1)}{x-1}$, then $k$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: Split the series into a G.P. ($x,x^2,\ldots$) and an A.P. ($k,k+2,\ldots$), then compare the $a$-parts.

alternate_solutions.idea: The identity holds for every $x\ne1$; put $x=0$ so that the G.P. part vanishes.
solution: Both expressions are equal for all $x\ne1$ and are polynomials in $x$ after cancelling $x-1$, so we may put $x=0$.
At $x=0$ the first $9$ terms reduce to $a\left[k+(k+2)+\ldots+(k+16)\right]=9(k+8)a$.

useful_results: A series whose terms are sums of two standard sequences splits into two standard sums ($\text{G.P.}+\text{A.P.}$).
The sum of $n$ terms of an A.P. is $n\times$ (middle term): here $9(k+8)$ since the middle (5th) term is $k+8$.
If two expressions are equal for all admissible $x$ you may substitute any convenient admissible value ($x=0$ here) to compare parts.

concepts: Arithmetic progression (sum of terms)
questions.question: If the first term of an A.P. is $3$ and the sum of its first $25$ terms is equal to the sum of its next $15$ terms, then the common difference of this A.P. is :
questions.key_idea: 'Next $15$ terms' means terms $26$ to $40$, so $S_{25}=S_{40}-S_{25}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Each block sum is (number of terms) $\times$ (middle term): $25\,a_{13}=15\,a_{33}$.
solution: $S_{25}=25\,a_{13}$ (middle term of terms $1$ to $25$ is the $13$th).
Terms $26$ to $40$ have $15$ terms with middle term $a_{33}$, so their sum is $15\,a_{33}$.

useful_results: Sum of consecutive terms of an A.P. $=$ (number of terms) $\times$ (middle term) $=$ $n\cdot a_{\text{middle}}$.
'Next $m$ terms' after the first $n$ are terms $n+1,\ldots,n+m$ with sum $S_{n+m}-S_n$.

concepts: Arithmetic progression (sum of $n$ terms, quadratic in $n$)
questions.question: If the sum of the series $20+19\frac35+19\frac15+18\frac45+\ldots$ up to $n^{th}$ term is $488$ and the $n^{th}$ term is negative, then :
questions.key_idea: $S_n=488$ is a quadratic in $n$ with two roots; the condition 'last term negative' selects the larger one.
solution: The series is an A.P. with $a=20$ and $d=-\frac25$ ($19\frac35=20-\frac25$).
The $n^{th}$ term is negative, so $n=61$ and $T_n=-4$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute each option into $T_n=20-\frac25(n-1)$ and $S_n=\frac n2(20+T_n)$.
solution: (C) $T_n=-4$ gives $n-1=60$, $n=61$, $S_{61}=\frac{61}{2}(20-4)=488$ and the term is negative. This is the answer.

useful_results: $S_n=\frac{n}{2}\left(2a+(n-1)d\right)$ is quadratic in $n$, so $S_n=\text{given value}$ can have two solutions; the extra condition (sign of last term) picks one.
$S_n$ of an A.P. is symmetric about the vertex $n=\frac12-\frac ad$; here $n=50.5$, so $S_{40}=S_{61}$ ($40+61=101$).
The terms change sign after $T_{51}=0$, so the partial sums rise to $S_{50}=S_{51}$ and then fall.

concepts: Arithmetic means and geometric means between two numbers
questions.question: If $m$ arithmetic means (A.Ms) and three geometric means (G.Ms) are inserted between $3$ and $243$ such that $4^{th}$ A.M. is equal to $2^{nd}$ G.M., then $m$ is equal to ______.
questions.key_idea: Three G.M.s make $3,G_1,G_2,G_3,243$ a G.P. with ratio $3$, so $G_2=27$; then $A_4=3+4d$ with $d=\frac{240}{m+1}$.
solution: $3,A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_m,243$ is an A.P. with common difference $d=\frac{243-3}{m+1}=\frac{240}{m+1}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $A_k$ lies $\frac{k}{m+1}$ of the way from $3$ to $243$; $G_2=27$ lies $\frac{24}{240}=\frac1{10}$ of the way.
solution: In the A.P. $3,A_1,\ldots,A_m,243$ there are $m+1$ equal steps, so $A_k=3+\frac{k}{m+1}(243-3)$.
In the G.P. $3,G_1,G_2,G_3,243$ the ratio is $3$, so $G_2=3\cdot3^2=27$.

useful_results: $n$ G.M.s between $a$ and $b$ have ratio $r=\left(\frac ba\right)^{\frac1{n+1}}$ and $G_k=ar^k$; $m$ A.M.s have $d=\frac{b-a}{m+1}$ and $A_k=a+kd$.
$A_k$ is the point at fraction $\frac{k}{m+1}$ of the way from $a$ to $b$ (linear interpolation).

concepts: Summation of series using $\sum r^2$ and $\sum r^3$
questions.question: If $1+(1-2^2\cdot1)+(1-4^2\cdot3)+(1-6^2\cdot5)+\ldots+(1-20^2\cdot19)=\alpha-220\beta$, then an ordered pair $(\alpha,\beta)$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: The $r$-th bracket is $1-(2r-1)(2r)^2$; expand and use $\sum r^3$ and $\sum r^2$ for $r=1..10$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Both power sums are multiples of $220$, so pull $220$ out and read $\alpha$ and $\beta$ from the remainder.
solution: Any other representation $\alpha-220\beta$ with the given options needs $\alpha\equiv11\pmod{220}$, so $\alpha=11$ (not $10$); then $\beta=103$.
The pair is $(11,103)$, the same answer.

useful_results: Sum over even numbers $2r$: $\sum(2r)^3=8\sum r^3$ and $\sum(2r)^2=4\sum r^2$.
When the answer has the form $\alpha-c\beta$, reduce mod $c$ first: $\alpha$ is the residue, which often decides between options.
Instance: the total is $-22649=11-220\times103$.

concepts: Arithmetic progression with integer common difference
questions.question: Let $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$ be a given A.P. whose common difference is an integer and $S_n=a_1+a_2+\ldots+a_n$. If $a_1=1$, $a_n=300$ and $15\le n\le50$, then the ordered pair $(S_{n-4},a_{n-4})$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: $d=\frac{299}{n-1}$ must be an integer, so $n-1$ divides $299=13\times23$; the range $15\le n\le50$ leaves one value.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the options: $d$ must divide both $299$ and $a_{n-4}-1$, so a $\gcd$ test picks the value of $a_{n-4}$.
solution: With $a_{n-4}=249$ we would need $d=1$, then $n=300\notin[15,50]$; so $a_{n-4}=248$ and $d=13$ (then $n-1=23$, $n=24$).
The pair is $(2490,248)$, the same answer.

useful_results: $a_n=a_1+(n-1)d$: an integer $d$ means $(n-1)\mid(a_n-a_1)$; list the divisors of $a_n-a_1$ and apply the range of $n$.
$S_m=\frac m2(a_1+a_m)$ needs only the first and last terms, not $d$.
Instance: $299=13\times23$, divisors $1,13,23,299$; only $n-1=23$ lies in $[14,49]$.

concepts: Geometric progression (positive terms, sum of $n$ terms)
questions.question: If the sum of the second, third and fourth terms of a positive term G.P. is $3$ and the sum of its sixth, seventh and eighth terms is $243$, then the sum of the first $50$ terms of this G.P. is :
questions.key_idea: Dividing the two given sums gives $r^4=81$; positivity of the terms gives $r=3$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Express $S_{50}$ as a multiple of the known sum $T_2+T_3+T_4$ so $a$ never has to be found.

useful_results: For a G.P., the ratio of two equal-length blocks of consecutive terms is $r^{k}$ where $k$ is the gap in their positions ($T_6/T_2=r^4$).
Any sum of a block of the G.P. is $a\,r^{j}\frac{r^m-1}{r-1}$, so $S_n$ and a block sum are related with $a$ eliminated.
'Positive terms' fixes the sign of $r$ when only $r^4$ is known.

concepts: Quadratic expression as a sum of squares
Geometric progression
questions.question: Let $a,b,c,d$ and $p$ be any non zero distinct real numbers such that $(a^2+b^2+c^2)p^2-2(ab+bc+cd)p+(b^2+c^2+d^2)=0$. Then :
questions.key_idea: The left side equals $(ap-b)^2+(bp-c)^2+(cp-d)^2$, a sum of squares that can vanish only if each square does.
solution: Hence $a,b,c,d$ are in G.P. (common ratio $p$): option (D).

alternate_solutions.idea: Treat it as a quadratic in $p$ with real root: discriminant $\ge0$ against Cauchy-Schwarz forces equality.
solution: The quadratic $Ap^2-2Bp+C=0$ with $A=a^2+b^2+c^2$, $B=ab+bc+cd$, $C=b^2+c^2+d^2$ has a real root $p$, so $B^2\ge AC$.
So $B^2=AC$, which is the equality case: $(a,b,c)$ and $(b,c,d)$ are proportional.
Hence $\frac ab=\frac bc=\frac cd$, so $a,b,c,d$ are in G.P., the same answer.

useful_results: $(a^2+b^2+c^2)p^2-2(ab+bc+cd)p+(b^2+c^2+d^2)=(ap-b)^2+(bp-c)^2+(cp-d)^2$: a recognition cue for a G.P. of four terms (ratio $p$).
Cauchy-Schwarz: $(ab+bc+cd)^2\le(a^2+b^2+c^2)(b^2+c^2+d^2)$ with equality iff $a:b:c=b:c:d$, i.e. $a,b,c,d$ in G.P.
Sum of squares of real numbers is $0$ iff each is $0$.
Same pattern with $n$ terms: $\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(a_ip-a_{i+1})^2=0\iff a_1,\ldots,a_n$ in G.P.

concepts: Arithmetic progression (two progressions, common difference)
questions.question: The common difference of the A.P. $b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_m$ is $2$ more than the common difference of A.P. $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$. If $a_{40}=-159$, $a_{100}=-399$ and $b_{100}=a_{70}$, then $b_1$ is equal to :
solution: Let $b_1,b_2,\ldots,b_m$ be A.P.$_1$ with difference $d_1$ and $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$ be A.P.$_2$ with difference $d_2$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's line 'a1 = -39 x 4 = -156' mislabels the quantity: $-39\times4=-156$ is $39d_2$, not $a_1$ (a_1 is $-3$, as the next lines correctly obtain). The working now writes $39d_2=-156$ and $a_1=-159+156=-3$. The PDF also jumps from $b_{100}=a_{70}$ to the numbers; the intermediate equation $b_1+99d_1=a_1+69d_2$ is written out. Answer $-81$ unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: $a_{70}$ is the midpoint of $a_{40}$ and $a_{100}$, so it is found without $a_1$.

useful_results: In an A.P., $a_{\frac{p+q}{2}}=\frac{a_p+a_q}{2}$ (the term midway in position is the mean of the two terms).
$d=\frac{a_q-a_p}{q-p}$ for any two terms.
$a_m=a_n+(m-n)d$ links any two terms without needing $a_1$.

concepts: AM-GM inequality (minimum value of an exponential expression)
questions.question: The minimum value of $f(x)=a^{a^x}+a^{1-a^x}$, where $a,x\in\mathbb R$ and $a>0$, is equal to :
questions.key_idea: The two terms $a^{a^x}$ and $a^{1-a^x}$ have constant product $a$, so AM-GM applies.
solution: Equality needs $a^{a^x}=a^{1-a^x}$, i.e. $a^x=\frac12$, which has the solution $x=\log_a\frac12$ (for $a=1$ both terms are $1$ and $f=2=2\sqrt a$).
So the minimum value is $2\sqrt a$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF stops at '$\ge2\sqrt a$' and calls it the minimum without showing that equality is attained. The equality step ($a^x=\frac12$, solvable for $a>0,a\ne1$; $a=1$ trivial) was added. Answer unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Let $t=a^x>0$; then $g(t)=a^t+a^{1-t}$ is convex and symmetric about $t=\frac12$, so its minimum is at $t=\frac12$.
solution: As $x$ varies over $\mathbb R$, $t=a^x$ takes every value in $(0,\infty)$ (for $a\ne1$). Write $g(t)=a^t+a^{1-t}$.

useful_results: If $u\cdot v$ is constant then $u+v\ge2\sqrt{uv}$ for $u,v>0$, with equality iff $u=v$.
Quantities of the form $\phi(t)+\phi(c-t)$ are symmetric about $t=\frac c2$; the extremum is at the centre when $\phi$ is convex.
Always check that equality is attainable inside the range ($a^x=\frac12$ needs $\frac12$ in the range $(0,\infty)$ of $a^x$).

concepts: Arithmetic progression
Determinants (row operations)
questions.question: If $x,y,z$ are in arithmetic progression with common difference $d$, $x\ne3d$, and the determinant of the matrix $\left[\begin{matrix}3&4\sqrt2&x\\4&5\sqrt2&y\\5&k&z\end{matrix}\right]$ is zero, then the value of $k^2$ is :
questions.key_idea: For $x,y,z$ in A.P., $R_2\to R_2-\frac{R_1+R_3}{2}$ makes the third entry of $R_2$ zero and the determinant factorises.
solution: Apply $R_2\to R_2-\frac{R_1+R_3}{2}$. Since $y-\frac{x+z}{2}=0$, the third entry of $R_2$ becomes $0$.
The factor $3z-5x=0$ would give $3(x+2d)-5x=0$, i.e. $x=3d$, which is excluded.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's expansion line prints the factor as $5\sqrt2-\frac{4\sqrt2+16}{2}$; the constant '16' is a misprint for $k$ (the middle entry of $R_2$ after the operation is $5\sqrt2-\frac{4\sqrt2+k}{2}$, as the PDF's own next lines use). Also the PDF writes $x\ne3d$ for the excluded case with $\lambda$ in place of $d$. Corrected to $k$ and $d$. Answer $72$ unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Split the third column as $x(1,1,1)^T+d(0,1,2)^T$ using linearity of the determinant.

useful_results: If $x,y,z$ are in A.P., then $R_2\to R_2-\frac{R_1+R_3}{2}$ (or $C_j$ analogue) produces a zero; the determinant factors.
Determinants are linear in each column: a column in A.P. equals $x\cdot\mathbf1+d\cdot(0,1,2)^T$, giving $x\Delta_1+d\Delta_2$.
Instance: the determinant equals $(x-3d)(k-6\sqrt2)$, so $x\ne3d$ is exactly the condition that makes $k$ unique.

concepts: Logarithms (change of base)
Arithmetic progression
questions.question: For three positive integers $p,q,r$, $x^{pq^2}=y^{qr}=z^{p^2r}$ and $r=pq+1$ such that $3,\ 3\log_yx,\ 3\log_zy,\ 7\log_xz$ are in A.P. with common difference $\frac12$. Then $r-p-q$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: The A.P. gives $\log_yx,\log_zy,\log_xz$; the equal powers give the same ratios in terms of $p,q,r$.
solution: $3\log_zy-3\log_yx=\frac12\Rightarrow\frac{3\log y}{\log z}-\frac{3\log x}{\log y}=\frac12\Rightarrow\frac{\log y}{\log z}=\frac43$ ...(2)
$7\log_xz-3\log_zy=\frac12\Rightarrow\frac{7\log z}{\log x}-\frac{3\log y}{\log z}=\frac12\Rightarrow\frac{\log z}{\log x}=\frac{9}{14}$ ...(3)
questions.correction_note: The PDF's equations (2) and (3) are misprinted. In (2) the second term is written $\frac{3\log y}{\log z}$ again instead of $\frac{3\log x}{\log y}$ (as printed the two terms would cancel and give $0=\frac12$); in (3) the second denominator is printed $\log2$ instead of $\log z$. The corrected forms are used; the results $\frac43$ and $\frac9{14}$, and the answer $2$, are unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Equation (5) with $r=pq+1$ gives $pq=6$ at once; then list the factor pairs and test one more ratio.

useful_results: If $x^{\alpha}=y^{\beta}=z^{\gamma}$ then $\alpha\ln x=\beta\ln y=\gamma\ln z$, so $\frac{\ln x}{\ln y}=\frac{\beta}{\alpha}$, etc.
The three ratios $\log_yx\cdot\log_zy\cdot\log_xz=1$ (cyclic product); check: $\frac76\cdot\frac43\cdot\frac9{14}=1$.
Integer-solution problems: get a product like $pq$ from one equation, list the finite factor pairs, and test one more equation.

concepts: Logarithms (change of base) and geometric progression
Arithmetic progression
questions.question: Let $a,b,c>1$, $a^3,b^3$ and $c^3$ be in A.P., $\log_ab$, $\log_ca$ and $\log_bc$ be in G.P. If the sum of first $20$ terms of an A.P., whose first term is $\frac{a+4b+c}{3}$ and the common difference is $\frac{a-8b+c}{10}$ is $-444$, then $abc$ is equal to
questions.key_idea: The G.P. of logarithms gives $(\log a)^3=(\log c)^3$, so $a=c$; the A.P. of cubes then gives $b=c$.
solution: $\log_ab,\log_ca,\log_bc$ in G.P.: $\left(\frac{\log a}{\log c}\right)^2=\frac{\log b}{\log a}\cdot\frac{\log c}{\log b}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $\log_ab\cdot\log_bc=\log_ac$ (chain rule), so the G.P. condition reads $(\log_ca)^2=\log_ac=\frac1{\log_ca}$; and the sum of an A.P. is $20\times$ its mean.
solution: The A.P. has first term $2t$ and $d=-\frac{3t}{5}$; its $20$-term sum is $20\times$ mean, and the mean is $T_1+9.5d=2t-5.7t=-3.7t$.

useful_results: Change of base chain: $\log_ab\cdot\log_bc=\log_ac$ and $\log_ab\cdot\log_ba=1$.
When $u^3=v^3$ for real $u,v$ then $u=v$; with $\log$ of bases $>1$ this gives equal numbers.
The sum of $n$ terms of an A.P. is $n\times$ mean, mean $=T_1+\frac{n-1}{2}d$.
Instance: $a=b=c=6$ makes the A.P. $12,\,8.4,\,\ldots$ with $S_{20}=-444$.

concepts: Counting selections with a given remainder
questions.question: The number of ways of selecting two numbers $a$ and $b$, $a\in\{2,4,6,\ldots,100\}$ and $b\in\{1,3,5,\ldots,99\}$ such that $2$ is the remainder when $a+b$ is divided by $23$ is
questions.key_idea: $a+b$ is odd and $\equiv2\pmod{23}$, so $a+b\in\{25,71,117,163\}$; count pairs for each sum.
solution: $a+b$ is odd and at most $199$, so $a+b$ can be $25,\ 71,\ 117,\ 163$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $a=2i$, $b=2j-1$ with $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,50\}$: the congruence becomes $i+j\equiv13\pmod{23}$.

useful_results: Number of pairs $(i,j)$ in $[1,n]^2$ with $i+j=s$ is $s-1$ for $2\le s\le n+1$ and $2n+1-s$ for $n+1\le s\le2n$.
Parity first: even $+$ odd is odd, so only odd values of $23\lambda+2$ (odd $\lambda$) are possible.
A congruence $2s\equiv c\pmod m$ with odd $m$ is solved by multiplying by the inverse of $2$.

concepts: Arithmetic progression
Minimum value of a quadratic expression
questions.question: Let $a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots$ be an A.P. If $a_7=3$, the product $a_1a_4$ is minimum and the sum of its first $n$ terms is zero, then $n!-4a_{n(n+2)}$ is equal to :
questions.key_idea: With $a_1=3-6d$ and $a_4=3-3d$ the product is a quadratic in $d$; its minimum fixes $d=\frac34$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The quadratic $a_1a_4$ vanishes at $d=\frac12$ and $d=1$, so its vertex is midway at $d=\frac34$; $S_n=0$ means $a_n=-a_1$.
solution: $a_1=3-6d$ is $0$ at $d=\frac12$, and $a_4=3-3d$ is $0$ at $d=1$; the product is an upward parabola with these roots.
The vertex is midway between the roots: $d=\frac{1/2+1}{2}=\frac34$, and $a_1=3-\frac92=-\frac32$.

useful_results: A quadratic $\alpha(d-r_1)(d-r_2)$ with $\alpha>0$ has its minimum at $d=\frac{r_1+r_2}{2}$.
$S_n=0$ for an A.P. with $d\ne0$ means $a_1+a_n=0$, i.e. the terms are symmetric about $0$.
$a_m=a_k+(m-k)d$ gives a far term directly from a known one.
Instance: $d=\frac34$, $a_1=-\frac32$; the terms $a_1,\ldots,a_5$ are $-\frac32,-\frac34,0,\frac34,\frac32$ with sum $0$.
